Building Your Touring Tool Kit

A well-assembled tool kit is like breakdown cover that travels at 60mph — it's there the instant you need it. You don't need to carry a full workshop, but the right selection of tools and spares can fix the most common roadside problems and keep your tour on track.

Core Tools

These tools should be tailored to your specific motorcycle. Before building your kit, check which fastener sizes your bike actually uses:

  • Multi-tool: A motorcycle-specific multi-tool (Cruztools, Motion Pro) combines several essentials in one compact package.
  • Socket set: A small 1/4" drive socket set with the sizes your bike uses. Most Japanese bikes use 8mm, 10mm, 12mm, 14mm.
  • Allen keys: A set from 3mm to 8mm. Many modern bikes use Allen head fasteners extensively.
  • Torx bits: Some European bikes (BMW, KTM) use Torx fasteners. Carry the sizes your bike needs.
  • Adjustable spanner: One small adjustable wrench covers gaps in your socket set.
  • Pliers: Needle-nose pliers for gripping, pulling, and electrical work.
  • Screwdrivers: Phillips and flat-head in medium size, or a multi-bit screwdriver.
  • Tyre levers: Two small tyre levers for puncture repair (if you carry a plug kit).

Tyre Repair

A puncture is the most common roadside emergency. Be ready for it:

  • Tubeless tyre repair kit: Plug kit with insertion tool, rubber cement, and a selection of plugs. Practice using it at home before you need it on the road.
  • CO2 inflators: Compact and fast. Carry at least 3 cartridges — one may not be enough for a large tyre.
  • Mini compressor (alternative): A 12V mini compressor powered from your bike's battery. Heavier but reusable and more versatile than CO2.
  • Tyre pressure gauge: A small dial gauge is more accurate than the markings on a compressor.

Spares Worth Carrying

  • Spare clutch lever: A snapped clutch lever ends your tour instantly. A spare weighs grams and takes minutes to fit.
  • Spare brake lever: Same logic as the clutch lever.
  • Bulbs: A headlight and indicator bulb for your specific bike. Quick, easy roadside repair.
  • Fuses: A selection matching your bike's fuse ratings. A blown fuse is a common cause of mysterious electrical failures.
  • Cable ties: The motorcyclist's duct tape. Fix fairings, secure cables, improvise repairs.
  • Gaffer tape: Strong, waterproof, incredibly versatile. Wrap some around a pencil to save space.
  • Wire: A short length of safety wire for emergency repairs.
The best tool kit is the one matched to your specific bike. Spend an hour at home identifying which fastener sizes your bike uses and build your kit around those sizes. Generic tool kits are heavy and half the tools won't fit your bike.

Fluids and Lubrication

  • Chain lube: A small can for re-lubing every 200-300 miles or after rain.
  • Small bottle of engine oil: 250ml in a secure container for top-ups.
  • WD-40 or equivalent: Displaces water, frees seized bolts, protects electrics.

Packing Your Tool Kit

Roll your tools in a tool roll or pack them in a small zip-lock bag. Keep them in an easily accessible part of your luggage — you don't want to unpack everything to reach your tools. Many riders keep the tool roll in a pannier pocket or strapped under the seat.

A 2kg tool kit that you've tailored to your bike could save a £200 recovery bill and a day off the road. It's the most weight-efficient investment in your entire touring setup.
keyTakeaways: Core tools should match your bike's fasteners: a multi-tool, Allen keys, Torx bits, an adjustable spanner, pliers, screwdrivers and tyre levers.
Carry a tubeless tyre repair kit with CO2 inflators or a mini compressor and a pressure gauge.
Worthwhile spares include clutch and brake levers, bulbs, fuses, cable ties, gaffer tape and wire.
Bring chain lube, a small bottle of engine oil and a can of WD-40.
Pack the kit low in a pannier and know how to use every item before you set off.

faq.q: What tools should I carry on a motorcycle tour?
faq.a: Carry a core set matched to your bike's fasteners: a good multi-tool, Allen keys, Torx bits, an adjustable spanner, pliers, screwdrivers and tyre levers. Add a tubeless tyre repair kit with CO2 inflators or a mini compressor and a pressure gauge. Do not carry tools for jobs you cannot do; if something major fails on a modern bike you are calling recovery anyway.

faq.q: Which spares are worth the space?
faq.a: Spare clutch and brake levers are worthwhile if your bike has exposed levers, since a snapped lever can strand you. Also carry spare bulbs and fuses, plenty of cable ties, gaffer tape and a length of wire. These lightweight items fix a surprising range of roadside problems and take up almost no room in a pannier.

faq.q: How do I fix a puncture on tour?
faq.a: Most touring tyres are tubeless, so carry a plug-style repair kit. Locate the puncture, ream the hole, insert a sticky plug, trim it, then reinflate using CO2 cartridges or a mini compressor. Check the pressure with a gauge and ride gently to the nearest tyre shop for a permanent repair or replacement.

faq.q: Where should I pack tools on the bike?
faq.a: Pack tools and other heavy items low and close to the bike's centre of gravity, ideally in a pannier rather than a tail pack, to keep handling stable. Keep the kit organised in a roll so items do not rattle loose, and make sure everything you carry is something you actually know how to use.
